flagship.headline: The Who blow up the Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour
flagship.summary_line_1: The Who closed My Generation on The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour by trashing their gear, and Keith Moon's bass drum, secretly packed with several times its normal explosive charge, detonated in a fireball that engulfed the stage.
flagship.summary_line_2: The blast threw Moon backward with cymbal shrapnel in his arm, singed Pete Townshend's hair, and briefly knocked the CBS broadcast off the air, a moment Townshend later blamed for the start of his lifelong hearing damage.

events.headline: Drake University paper prints the first Paul is Dead story
events.summary_line_1: Student editor Tim Harper's article Is Beatle Paul McCartney Dead? ran in Drake University's Times-Delphic, cataloging clues fans claimed were hidden across recent Beatles albums, including the backward message some heard in Revolution 9.
events.summary_line_2: Picked up by other college papers and Detroit radio within weeks, it became the first printed account of the biggest hoax in rock history, all built around a Beatle who was very much alive.

events.headline: Astrud Gilberto tracks her album at Century Sound Studios
events.summary_line_1: Bossa nova singer Astrud Gilberto recorded her seventh studio album at Century Sound Studios in New York with producer Brooks Arthur, later naming the record simply after that day, September 17, 1969.
events.summary_line_2: The album leaned on late-1960s pop covers like Chicago's Beginnings, folding her airy Brazilian phrasing into the string-heavy easy listening sound then dominating adult pop radio.

events.headline: Diana Ross and the Supremes track Love Child
events.summary_line_1: Diana Ross and the Supremes began recording Love Child at Hitsville U.S.A., a socially conscious single about growing up out of wedlock written and produced by Motown's newly formed songwriting team The Clan.
events.summary_line_2: Only Ross sang on the finished record, and the single became the group's eleventh number one, knocking the Beatles' Hey Jude off the top of the US chart weeks later.

events.headline: The Who blow up the Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour
events.summary_line_1: The Who closed My Generation on The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour by trashing their gear, and Keith Moon's bass drum, secretly packed with several times its normal explosive charge, detonated in a fireball that engulfed the stage.
events.summary_line_2: The blast threw Moon backward with cymbal shrapnel in his arm, singed Pete Townshend's hair, and briefly knocked the CBS broadcast off the air, a moment Townshend later blamed for the start of his lifelong hearing damage.

events.headline: The Doors get banned from The Ed Sullivan Show
events.summary_line_1: The Doors performed People Are Strange and Light My Fire live on The Ed Sullivan Show, and Jim Morrison ignored the producers' demand to swap the word higher for better and sang the original lyric straight into the camera.
events.summary_line_2: A furious Ed Sullivan scrapped the band's contract for six future appearances on the spot, and Morrison later shrugged it off, saying they had already done the Sullivan show.

events.headline: Johnny Rivers' Poor Side of Town debuts on the Hot 100
events.summary_line_1: Johnny Rivers' self-written ballad Poor Side of Town made its first appearance on the Billboard Hot 100, a lush, orchestrated turn away from the live go-go covers that had made his name.
events.summary_line_2: Written with producer Lou Adler for the album Changes, the song climbed to number one by November, Rivers' only chart-topper of the decade.

events.headline: The Vince Guaraldi Trio tracks A Charlie Brown Christmas
events.summary_line_1: The Vince Guaraldi Trio began sessions at Fantasy Studios in San Francisco for the CBS special A Charlie Brown Christmas, cutting early takes of Christmas Is Coming and Skating alongside the instrumental Christmas Time Is Here.
events.summary_line_2: The resulting soundtrack has since sold five times platinum, permanently welding cool jazz piano trio arrangements to a holiday television tradition.

events.headline: The Beatles collect a record $150,000 payday in Kansas City
events.summary_line_1: The Beatles played Municipal Stadium after Kansas City Athletics owner Charles O. Finley personally guaranteed $150,000, more than any act had ever been paid for a single show, opening the set fittingly with Kansas City / Hey-Hey-Hey-Hey.
events.summary_line_2: Attendance fell well short of the stadium's capacity due to local resentment toward Finley, and the promoter is believed to have lost tens of thousands of dollars on the gamble.

events.headline: Be My Baby tops the WABC survey over two soon-to-be classics
events.summary_line_1: The Ronettes' Be My Baby took the number one spot on the WABC Musicradio survey, edging out The Angels' My Boyfriend's Back at number two and Bobby Vinton's Blue Velvet at number three.
events.summary_line_2: Phil Spector's Wall of Sound production on Be My Baby went on to influence a generation of songwriters, with Brian Wilson famously calling it the greatest record ever made.

events.headline: Arthur Alexander releases Anna (Go to Him)
events.summary_line_1: Dot Records released Arthur Alexander's Anna (Go to Him), a country-soul ballad he wrote and sang with a vulnerable, aching delivery that reached the R&B top ten.
events.summary_line_2: The song's biggest legacy came a year later when the Beatles covered it for Please Please Me, with John Lennon modeling his lead vocal directly on Alexander's original.

events.headline: Sam Phillips opens his new Madison Avenue studio
events.summary_line_1: Sun Records founder Sam Phillips opened the Sam C. Phillips Recording Service at 639 Madison Avenue in Memphis, a custom-built facility that replaced the cramped original Sun Studio at 706 Union Avenue.
events.summary_line_2: Phillips financed the expansion partly on the strength of Charlie Rich's 1960 Phillips International hit Lonely Weekends, and the new studio became the label's recording home for the rest of the decade.
